result.summary:
Rework iteration 1 of 3 on docs/agents/test-specs/REQ-021.md, addressing the single MAJOR finding in handoffs/WF02-REQ-021/step-03b-test-design-validator.json: AC2b's tie-break case was written as a script meant to be re-run 3 times as 3 SEPARATE `npx tsx` process invocations to prove order-independence, but its fixture (chapter code literal 'r21a2script', plus users seeded the same way) used fixed, non-varying identifiers with no cleanup step and no cross-process uniqueness strategy. apps/bot/src/db/schema.ts's `chapters_code_unique` (line 54) and `users_tg_id_unique` (line 94) would reject run 2 and run 3 as duplicates of what run 1 already committed, crashing on a real unique-constraint violation instead of exercising the intended property -- forcing TEST-RUNNER to invent a fix, which Step 3b's check (c) prohibits.

Read the section named in the finding (docs/agents/test-specs/REQ-021.md lines 221-253) in full, and read apps/bot/src/domain/registration.db.test.ts lines 52-83 to confirm this project's established idiom for generating unique fixture values: module-level counters (`chapterSeq`, `userSeq`, `tgSeq`) that increment per call within a single process, restarting from a fixed base only on a fresh process start -- confirming the validator's point that this idiom, reused verbatim, does NOT survive separate process invocations, and that the fix has to either avoid relying on process-restart-safe uniqueness or avoid the multi-process structure altogether.

Chose option (c) from the rework instructions: restructured AC2b to run its 3 order-independence repetitions as 3 loop iterations INSIDE one script invocation/one process, rather than 3 separate `npx tsx` process launches. Each loop iteration seeds its own wholly fresh chapter (via a script-local `tieIterSeq` counter producing chapter codes `r21a2-tie-1`/`-2`/`-3`), its own fresh published event, and its own fresh pair of users (tg_ids derived from the same counter), then performs the identical-`created_at` two-row insert and tie-break check against that iteration's own event. This was chosen over (a) timestamp/random-suffixed identifiers and (b) an explicit cross-run DELETE step because: it requires no wall-clock or randomness dependency (staying consistent with the rest of this spec's preference for exact literals over `Date.now()`-based values, e.g. AC2a's fixed `2026-11-01T00:00:1{0,20,30}.000Z` timestamps), it needs no new cleanup instruction (nothing to clean up between iterations since each iteration's fixture is already disjoint by construction, mirroring registration.db.test.ts's own counter idiom exactly), and it sidesteps the cross-process uniqueness problem entirely rather than solving it -- since AC2a and AC2c already run inside this same single script invocation with no re-run requirement, keeping AC2b's repetition inside that same process is also the more consistent fit with the rest of the spec's structure. The property under test (order-independence of the tie-break across separate 2-row `INSERT ... VALUES` statements, since Postgres's physical row-return order for a multi-row VALUES insert is not guaranteed) is preserved undiminished: each loop iteration is a genuinely independent, freshly-seeded 2-row insert into an otherwise-empty event, so Postgres is equally free to return rows in either order on each of the 3 iterations -- nothing pins or biases the outcome toward passing.

Updated the AC2 row of the coverage table (docs/agents/test-specs/REQ-021.md, Coverage table section) to describe AC2b as '3 independently-seeded loop iterations inside one script invocation' instead of 'run 3x for order-independence', and to note that a non-deterministic/duplicate tie-break position on ANY of the 3 iterations fails the case (not just an aggregate one-shot check).

No other section changed: AC1, AC2a, AC2c, AC3, AC4, AC-catalog, the shared setup, and the coverage table's AC1/AC3/AC4 rows are untouched, matching the task instruction to touch only AC2b (and the AC2 coverage-table row for consistency, since it described the now-removed 3-process-re-run mechanic).
